questions.question_text: A 48-year-old man presents to a psychiatrist, stating that he was pressured by his wife to seek help. He explains that he likes to collect wine, and he does not see a problem with this; he claims that many of the wines are quite valuable and a potential investment. On further questioning, he admits that he rarely drinks the wines, because it “never seems the right time.” He has never sold or given away any wine because he finds it hard to part with the bottles. He has had to use increasing portions of his house for storage of the wine, which, along with the financial hardship, is his wife’s primary concern. He admits that many of the wine bottles have probably spoiled because he cannot afford to properly store the wine and the bottles have sat for years on shelves. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of normal collecting behavior.
A diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder.

questions.explanation: Although wine collecting is not in itself pathological, in this case the patient’s difficulty parting with or drinking the wine, the fact that his acquisition exceeds his ability to store the wine, and his wife’s distress (along with a possible financial impact) make hoarding disorder the most likely diagnosis. Hoarding disorder describes a syndrome in which an individual has difficulty parting with possessions, to the point that the possessions present an unsafe or unhygienic situation. Approximately 80%–90% of individuals with hoarding disorder also display excessive acquisition in which they collect, buy, or steal objects that are not needed and for which there is no space. In such cases, this is indicated with a specifier. Although persons with obsessivecompulsive disorder may hoard items, they usually experience distress at their inability to throw the objects away, or their storage of the possessions serves some other purpose related to their obsessions (e.g., worrying that they will throw out something important).

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which disorders is included in the “Anxiety Disorders” chapter of DSM-5?

options.text: A diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder.
A diagnosis of acute stress disorder.
A diagnosis of panic disorder with agoraphobia.
A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: The DSM-5 “Anxiety Disorders” chapter contains a number of additions and deletions when compared with the prior edition. A number of anxiety disorders classified by DSM-IV as disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence are now included among the DSM-5 anxiety disorders, including separation anxiety disorder and selective mutism. Several DSM-IV disorders from the “Anxiety Disorders” chapter, including obsessivecompulsive disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, and acute stress disorder, were removed from that section in DSM-5. This reorganization was the result of a scientific review that concluded that these were distinct disorders that were not sufficiently described by the presence of anxiety symptoms. Agoraphobia has been separated from panic disorder as a distinct disorder in DSM5, which includes a panic attack specifier when they co-occur.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old retail worker believes that he has “chronic halitosis” and fears that his bad breath is “scaring away shoppers.” He is in danger of losing his job because he so frequently absents himself from the sales floor to brush his teeth and use mouthwash. He constantly chews mint gum, even though his employer has asked him not to. His coworkers regularly reassure him that his Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 59 breath is fine, but he is convinced that they are just being polite. Although the possibility of losing his job causes him concern, he finds his worries about his breath to be intolerable. He has seen his doctor and dentist, both of whom tell him that he is healthy and does not have malodorous breath. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder.
Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder.
A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.

correct_answer.text: Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder.

questions.explanation: Olfactory reference syndrome is characterized by excessive odorrelated preoccupations and repetitive behaviors designed to address the odor sufficient to cause distress or impairment. Currently this disorder is provisional and classified under other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. When the individual lacks any insight, a delusional disorder should be diagnosed as well. Although the other disorders listed could cause repetitive behaviors, the focus on an imaginary odor is diagnostic for olfactory reference syndrome.

questions.question_text: A man is told he needs foot amputation and is admitted to hospital. He sees a patient who has had similar surgery, becomes distressed, breaks equipment, and says death is better than this. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The acute distress response following a severe identified stressor (amputation) with behavioral dyscontrol indicates an acute stress reaction occurring shortly after the stressor.

questions.question_text: The determination of whether a panic attack is expected or unexpected is ultimately best made by which of the following?

options.text: A diagnosis of careful clinical judgment.
Whether the patient attributes the panic to external versus internal causes.
Whether panic attacks occur primarily during the day versus at night.
Whether the attacks occur in response to cultural or religious practices.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of careful clinical judgment.

questions.explanation: It can be difficult to determine whether panic attacks are expected (i.e., triggered by some external stress or situation). Patients (particularly older individuals) may retrospectively attribute panic attacks to certain stressful situations even if they were unexpected in the moment. Laboratory 260 | Anxiety Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE testing may rule out other potential medical causes. Agents with disparate mechanisms of action, such as sodium lactate, caffeine, isoproterenol, yohimbine, carbon dioxide, or cholecystokinin, provoke panic attacks in individuals with panic disorder to a much greater extent than in healthy control subjects (and in some cases, than in individuals with other anxiety, depressive, or bipolar disorders without panic attacks). In a proportion of individuals with panic disorder, panic attacks are related to hypersensitive medullary carbon dioxide detectors, resulting in hypocapnia and other respiratory irregularities; however, none of these laboratory findings are considered diagnostic of panic disorder. There is no definitive test; ultimately the determination is based on a clinical judgment that takes into account the sequence of events leading to the attack, the patient’s own sense of whether triggers are present, and potential cultural factors that may influence a determination of cause.

questions.question_text: Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) differs from normative shyness in that the disorder leads to which of the following?

options.text: A diagnosis of social or occupational dysfunction.
A diagnosis of marked social reticence.
A diagnosis of avoidance of social situations.
A diagnosis of derealization or depersonalization.
Chronic avoidance of most interpersonal situations despite desired social engagement.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of social or occupational dysfunction.

questions.explanation: Shyness (i.e., social reticence) is a common personality trait and is not by itself pathological. In some societies, shyness is even evaluated positively. However, when there is a significant adverse impact on social, occupational, and other important areas of functioning, a diagnosis of social anxiety disorder should be considered, and when full diagnostic criteria for social anxAnxiety Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 267 iety disorder are met, the disorder should be diagnosed. Only a minority (12%) of self-identified shy individuals in the United States have symptoms that meet diagnostic criteria for social anxiety disorder.

questions.question_text: What is the most common anatomical site of hair pulling in trichotillomania?
questions.explanation: Trichotillomania can involve any area of the body, but the most common sites are the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelids.

questions.question_text: Which is a distinguishing feature of complex PTSD compared to PTSD?
questions.explanation: Complex PTSD includes distinctive features such as decreased self-worth, affective dysregulation, poor interpersonal relationships, and is associated with repetitive trauma exposure.

questions.question_text: A 52-year-old man with raw, chapped hands is referred to a psychiatrist by his primary care doctor. The man reports that he washes his hands repeatedly, spending up to 4 hours a day, using abrasive cleansers and scalding hot water. Although he admits that his hands are uncomfortable, he is entirely convinced that unless he washes in this manner he will become gravely ill. A medical workup is unrevealing, and the man takes no medications. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of delusional disorder, somatic type.
A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder.
A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: DSM-5 has added an insight specifier to the diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) to acknowledge that persons with the disorder can range from having good insight into the irrationality of their behaviors to having no insight (i.e., being delusional). In DSM-5, if the delusional belief is limited to the obsessions and compulsions, a separate psychotic disorder diagnosis is not required. Individuals with illness anxiety disorder worry about having an illness; however, they do not have the classic obsessions and compulsions found in OCD. Individuals with generalized anxiety disorder may constantly worry; however, their worries are usually about real-life concerns. Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder is not characterized by intrusive thoughts, images, or urges or by repetitive behaviors that are performed in response to these intrusions; instead, it involves an enduring and pervasive maladaptive pattern of excessive perfectionism and rigid control.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old man has regularly experienced panic attacks when out of his home alone and when on the bus. He now avoids leaving home for fear of experiencing these attacks. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of panic disorder with agoraphobia.
A diagnosis of agoraphobia with panic attacks.
A diagnosis of specific phobia, situational type.
Two separate disorders: panic disorder and agoraphobia.

correct_answer.text: Two separate disorders: panic disorder and agoraphobia.

questions.explanation: This man has panic disorder, not just panic attacks, and he also has agoraphobia. Whereas DSM-IV considered the co-occurrence of panic and agoraphobia as a subtype of panic attacks, agoraphobia with or without panic is now a separate diagnosis; the presence of panic attacks can be indicated by a specifier. In specific phobia, the fear would be of the situation itself rather than the possibility of having a panic attack.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of obsessions is most commonly associated with obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD)?
questions.explanation: The most common pattern in OCD is an obsession of contamination, which is often followed by washing or compulsive avoidance of the contaminated object. Pathologic doubt is the second most common obsession seen in OCD.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which factors would support a physiological cause of anxiety in medically ill older adults, rather than a psychological cause?

options.text: The individual has experienced a major life change.
The individual has high scores on measures of neuroticism.
Anxiety symptoms arise in the absence of psychiatric history or risk factors.
There are no new medications or lapses in medication adherence.

correct_answer.text: Anxiety symptoms arise in the absence of psychiatric history or risk factors.

questions.explanation: The relationship of anxiety and medical illness is complex, as many physical illnesses and medications in late life cause 222 • PSYCHIATRY anxiety symptoms on a physiological level, but patients often have a psychological response to the diagnosis of medical illness as well. If anxiety symptoms arise in the absence of psychiatric history or risk factors, a physiological cause should be considered. The other factors would be supportive of psychological origins of anxiety. questions.explanation: Trichotillomania can involve any area of the body, but the most common sites are scalp, eyebrows, and eyelids.

questions.question_text: Which brain structure is most implicated in the pathophysiology of PTSD?
questions.explanation: The amygdala is most implicated in PTSD, particularly due to its role in fear response and consolidation of emotional memories, with reduced bilateral amygdala volume commonly observed.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated lifetime prevalence of blood-injection-injury phobia?
questions.explanation: The estimated lifetime prevalence of blood-injection-injury phobia is around 3.5%. This is a direct factual statement requiring simple recall.

questions.question_text: A veteran exposed to combat one year ago presents with re-experiencing symptoms, avoidance of loud noises, nightmares, but maintains good self-image and positive relationships. The appropriate ICD-11 diagnosis is:

options.text: Other Specified Trauma or Stress-Related Disorder

questions.explanation: This presentation meets criteria for PTSD with re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal symptoms. The maintained self-image and relationships differentiate it from CPTSD.

questions.question_text: From a psychopharmacological treatment perspective, what matters most when selecting treatment for a patient with an anxiety disorder?

options.text: The duration of illness before treatment initiation
The family history of anxiety or depressive disorders
The patient's insight into their condition
The specific symptoms the patient is experiencing, matched to malfunctioning brain circuits
Whether the patient meets full diagnostic criteria for a DSM category

correct_answer.text: The specific symptoms the patient is experiencing, matched to malfunctioning brain circuits

questions.explanation: The brain is organised according to circuits with topographical localisation of function, not according to diagnostic manuals. Treatment is therefore most rationally selected by deconstructing the patient's presentation into its specific symptoms, matching each symptom to the hypothetically malfunctioning brain circuit that underlies it, identifying the relevant neurotransmitters, and selecting agents that target those systems. This symptom-based approach is often more clinically useful than relying solely on categorical diagnosis.

questions.question_text: An adolescent who is an alcoholic drinker is hesitant to go out with parents, fearing they may vomit at a party. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) involves fear of social situations and scrutiny, though alcohol dependence is also present as a complicating factor.

questions.question_text: According to the National Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (1995), what was the most common anxiety disorder identified in the UK?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that in the NPMS, the most common anxiety disorder was mixed anxiety-depression followed by GAD. While phobic disorder was most common in the ECA and NCS studies from the USA, the NPMS data showed a different prevalence pattern for UK populations.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is more suggestive of anxiety that is not pathological than of anxiety that qualifies for a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder?

options.text: Anxiety and worry that is limited to specific, easily identifiable situations.
Anxiety that typically lasts for only a few days or weeks.
Anxiety and worry in response to a clear precipitant.
Worry that focuses on a single area of life concern.
Symptoms that appear suddenly without any preceding stress.

correct_answer.text: Anxiety and worry in response to a clear precipitant.

questions.explanation: Several features distinguish generalized anxiety disorder from anxiety that is not pathological. First, the worries associated with generalized anxiety disorder are more pervasive, pronounced, and distressing; have longer duration; and frequently occur without precipitants. Second, the worries associated with generalized anxiety disorder are excessive and typically interfere significantly with psychosocial functioning, whereas the worries of everyday life are not excessive and are perceived as more manageable and may be put off when more pressing matters arise. The greater the range of life circumstances about which a person worries (e.g., finances, children’s safety, job performance), the more likely his or her symptoms are to meet criteria for generalized anxiety disorder. Third, everyday worries are much less likely to be accompanied by physical symptoms (e.g., restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge). Individuals with generalized anxiety disorder report subjective distress due to constant worry and related impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

questions.question_text: Massed negative practice treatment is used in the treatment of

options.text: A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: Massed negative practice requires the individual to deliberately perform the tic accurately and with effort for a specifi c amount of time during the day. In theory, this is supposed to induce conditioned inhibition or conditioned fatigue of the behaviour, which results in a decrease in the tic. This is usually employed when habit reversal techniques have not been found to be useful. The evidence for the effectiveness of this treatment is not compelling, especially when compared with habit reversal training. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 168.

questions.question_text: In addition to feeling restless or “keyed up,” patients with generalized anxiety disorder are most likely to experience which of the following symptoms?

options.text: A diagnosis of multiple somatic complaints.

questions.explanation: Generalized anxiety disorder is defined as excessive anxiety and worry that occurs more days than not, lasts for at least 6 months, and is associated with restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge and muscle tension. The anxiety cannot be due to other anxiety disorders; the symptoms listed in the other options suggest other disorders that would be part of the differential diagnosis (i.e., panic disorder [option A], obsessive-compulsive disorder [option B], somatic symptom disorder [option D], and social anxiety disorder [social phobia] [option E]).

questions.question_text: Social Anxiety - Adult Comorbidity A patient with social anxiety disorder in adolescence is now an adult. Comorbid conditions are reviewed. Which comorbidity becomes particularly prominent in adults with social anxiety?
questions.explanation: Substance misuse (especially alcohol) commonly develops in adults with social anxiety as a maladaptive coping mechanism.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which distinguishes acute stress disorder (ASD) from PTSD?

options.text: Dissociative features may be diagnosed in PTSD but not ASD.
Significant distress is required for PTSD but not ASD.
The index trauma must be directly experienced in PTSD but not ASD.

correct_answer.text: Significant distress is required for PTSD but not ASD.

questions.explanation: In DSM5, a new chapter on disruptive, impulse control, and conduct disorders includes oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), conduct disorder (CD), intermittent explosive disorder (IED), pyromania, and kleptomania. This is a change from DSM-I V-T R, in which IED, pyromania, and kleptomania were included under “impulse control disorders not elsewhere classified,” and ODD and CD under “disorders first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence.” Trichotillomania (or skinpicking disorder) was previously included under “impulse control disorders not elsewhere classified” but has been recategorized to the obsessive– compulsive and related disorders label in DSM5.

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old boy cannot go to sleep without having a parent in his room and frequently awakens to check that a parent is still there. If he wakes up alone, he panics and searches for his parents. He reports frequent nightmares in which his parents are harmed. He becomes extremely distressed in anticipation of being left with a relative when his parents attempt to go on vacation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The essential feature of separation anxiety disorder is excessive anxiety about being separated from home or attachment figures, beyond what would be expected for the person’s developmental stage. Children frequently have difficulty at bedtime and may insist that a parent stay with them, often expressing fear of harm or untoward events preventing them from being with a loved one.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder has been taking sertraline 200mg daily for 12 weeks with minimal improvement. Her symptoms significantly impair her daily functioning. Which medication is most appropriate to add as augmentation?

questions.question_text: Maria has obsessive thoughts of a violent nature towards her mother. Which of the following is the least characteristic of dysfunctional assumptions likely to be seen in Maria?

options.text: Intrusive violent thoughts are equivalent to performing the violent act
The individual must maintain strict control over all thoughts
Holding a thought while believing you won't act on it still makes you responsible for it
Failure to suppress or counter a violent thought indicates desire to commit the violence
If I don’t please everyone, I am a failure

correct_answer.text: If I don’t please everyone, I am a failure

questions.explanation: Salkovskis described fi ve characteristic dysfunctional assumptions in patients with obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD). The fi rst option refers to thought–action fusion, i.e. having a thought equates to performing the action. This is consistent with the thoughts of patients with OCD, especially those who have ‘violent’ obsessions. The second statement that a person should (and can) exercise control over one’s thoughts is also consistent with thoughts in OCD. Responsibility is not attenuated by other factors (e.g. the low probability of occurrence) is a typical assumption in patients with OCD. The fourth option is also typical of an obsessive cognition. The fi nal option is an assumption that is not typical of OCD. This is probably more typical of a depressive assumption that reinforces the core belief ‘I am a failure’. As a corollary, there may be another secondary assumption – ‘If I please everyone, I am considered successful’. Freeman C and Power M. Handbook of Evidence-based Psychotherapies: A Guide for Research and Practice, 1st edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 146.

questions.explanation: That Psychological therapy is more effective than pharmacological therapy and should be used as first line where possible, making it the recommended first-line intervention according to NICE guidelines.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of anxiety disorder due to another medical condition is clinically significant anxiety that is judged to be best explained as a physiological effect of another medical condition. Symptoms can include prominent anxiety symptoms or panic attacks (Criterion A). The judgment that Anxiety Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 271 the symptoms are best explained by the associated physical condition must be based on evidence from the history, physical examination, or laboratory findings. In individuals who have serious medical illness and comorbid anxiety symptoms, anxiety disorder due to another medical condition is a potential cause. Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition is more likely to have a physical component of the anxiety than are the adjustment disorders. Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition should be distinguished from adjustment disorders, with anxiety, or with anxiety and depressed mood. Adjustment disorder is warranted when individuals experience a maladaptive response to the stress of having another medical condition. The reaction to stress usually concerns the meaning or consequences of the stress, as compared with the experience of anxiety or mood symptoms that occur as a physiological consequence of the other medical condition. In adjustment disorder, the anxiety symptoms are typically related to coping with the stress of having a general medical condition, whereas in anxiety disorder due to another medical condition, individuals are more likely to have prominent physical symptoms and to be focused on issues other than the stress of the illness itself.

questions.question_text: OCD symptoms may be reduced by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Fluvoxamine and sertraline, Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) Therapy, and cognitive restructuring 288 • PsyChiatRy (i.e., during cognitive behavioral therapy) are all evidencebased methods to treat OCD. Clonazepam is not generally used to treat underlying, core symptoms of OCD.

questions.question_text: Men with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) differ from women with the disorder in which of the following ways?

options.text: Women tend to get OCD earlier in life.
Men are more frequently reported to have comorbid tics.
Men are more commonly identified as obsessed with cleaning.
Men are more frequently observed to spontaneously recover.
OCD has equal prevalence in men and women.

correct_answer.text: Men are more frequently reported to have comorbid tics.

questions.explanation: Males have an earlier age at onset of OCD than females and are more likely to have comorbid tic disorders. Gender differences in the pattern of symptom dimensions have been reported, with, for example, females more likely to have symptoms in the cleaning dimension and males more likely to have symptoms in the forbidden thoughts and symmetry dimensions. The 12-month prevalence of OCD in the United States is 1.2%, with a similar prevalence internationally (1.1%–1.8%). Females are affected at a slightly higher rate than males in adulthood, although males are more commonly affected in childhood. For both genders, the course of OCD is usually chronic, often with waxing and waning symptoms. Without treatment, remission rates in adults are low (e.g., 20% for those reevaluated 40 years later).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT listed as an OCD spectrum disorder associated with somatic preoccupation?

options.text: All of the above are listed

questions.explanation: The source lists somatic preoccupation disorders as body dysmorphic disorder, hypochondriasis or anorexia nervosa, while trichotillomania is categorized under impulse control disorders, not somatic preoccupation disorders.

questions.question_text: Which characteristic distinguishes complex PTSD from typical PTSD?

options.text: Exposure to prolonged or repeated traumatic events

correct_answer.text: Exposure to prolonged or repeated traumatic events

questions.explanation: Complex PTSD is related to a series of traumatic events over time or one prolonged event, whereas typical PTSD arises after a single traumatic episode.

questions.question_text: Criterion A4 of posttraumatic stress disorder requires “Experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the traumatic event.” which of the following options would not qualify as an experiencing trauma under this criterion?

options.text: Voluntary recall of traumatic memories during therapy sessions.
Deliberate imaginative flooding as part of trauma-focused treatment.
Thinking about warning signs that preceded the traumatic event.
A college student at a film festival watching a series of violent movies that contain graphic rape scenes.
Conscious efforts to write down details of the trauma for processing.

correct_answer.text: A college student at a film festival watching a series of violent movies that contain graphic rape scenes.

questions.explanation: The examples given in Criterion A4 of posttraumatic stress disorder are first responders collecting human remains and police officers repeatedly exposed to details of child abuse. This criterion does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies, or pictures, unless the exposure is work related.

questions.question_text: Criterion B for acute stress disorder requires the presence of nine (or more) symptoms from any of five categories of response. which of the following options is not one of these five categories?
questions.explanation: Criterion B for acute stress disorder requires the presence of 9 (or more) of a total of 12 symptoms from any of the five categories of intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal, beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred.

questions.question_text: A woman's daughter is undergoing chemotherapy for 3 months. The woman has discussed this with friends and family, and it reminds her of her mother's death from cancer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adjustment disorder is characterized by maladaptive reaction to an identifiable psychosocial stressor that usually emerges within a month of the stressor, with preoccupation with the stressor and failure to adapt causing significant impairment, typically resolving within 6 months.

questions.question_text: In social anxiety disorder (social phobia), what is the primary object of an individual's fear?
questions.explanation: In social anxiety disorder, an individual experiences fear or anxiety in situations in which he or she is exposed to scrutiny, with the fear being that this may result in humiliation, embarrassment, or offense to others.

questions.question_text: Eighteen months following the death of her son in a skiing accident, a 49-year-old woman consults you for psychotherapy. She is preoccupied with the death, blames herself for providing the trip as a gift, and describes intense yearning for her son. She has not entered his room since his death, feels anger toward her husband, and is socially isolated. A 6-month trial of a full-dose SSRI had no impact. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: Other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder

correct_answer.text: Other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder

questions.explanation: The severe and persistent grief and mourning reactions characterize a symptom presentation meeting criteria for the proposed diagnosis persistent complex bereavement disorder. Because this is in Section III of DSM-5, the appropriate clinical diagnosis is other specified trauma- and stressor-related disorder.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which most accurately describes people with specific phobias?

options.text: The average patients with a phobia has fears of only one object or situation.
The fear is commonly quite mild in intensity.
Approximately 50% of phobia sufferers fear multiple objects or situations.
The fear occurs almost every time the person encounters the object or situation.
The fear intensity varies considerably depending on context and emotional state.

correct_answer.text: The fear occurs almost every time the person encounters the object or situation.

questions.explanation: A key feature of specific phobia is that the fear or anxiety is circumscribed to the presence of a particular situation or object (Criterion A), which may be termed the phobic stimulus. Categories of feared situations or objects (i.e., phobic stimuli) are provided as specifiers in the diagnostic criteria. Many individuals fear objects or situations from more than one category. For the diagnosis of specific phobia, the response must differ from normal, transient fears that commonly occur in the population. To meet the criteria for a diagnosis, the fear or anxiety must be intense or severe (i.e., “marked”; Criterion A). The amount of fear experienced may vary with proximity to the feared object or situation and may occur in anticipation of or in the actual presence of the object or situation. Also, the fear or anxiety may take the form of a full or limited-symptom panic attack (i.e., expected panic attack). Another characteristic of specific phobias is that fear or anxiety is evoked nearly every time the individual comes into contact with the phobic stimulus (Criterion B). Thus, an individual who becomes anxious only occasionally upon being confronted with the situation or object (e.g., becomes anxious when flying only on one out of every five airplane flights) would not be diagnosed with specific phobia. However, the degree of fear or anxiety expressed may vary (from anticipatory anxiety to a full panic attack) across different occasions of encountering the phobic object or situation because of various contextual factors, such as the presence of others, duration of exposure, and other threatening elements such as turbulence on a flight for individuals who fear flying.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is accurate regarding physiological characteristics of individuals with panic disorder?

options.text: At rest, individuals with panic disorder have increased autonomic arousal relative to healthy individuals.
individuals with panic disorder have autonomic arousal during panic attacks but return to a normal baseline following the attack.
individuals with panic disorder have autonomic arousal during panic attacks and for a period of roughly 60 minutes following the attack, which then resolves.
At rest, individuals with panic disorder have less autonomic arousal than individuals with generalized anxiety disorder.

correct_answer.text: At rest, individuals with panic disorder have increased autonomic arousal relative to healthy individuals.

questions.explanation: Patients with panic disorder, although they may feel calm between panic attacks, have increased autonomic arousal relative to healthy individuals. They also have more autonomic arousal at rest than do patients with generalized anxiety disorder. Re FeRe NCe Grillon, C., & Cornwell, B. R. (2009). Anxiety disorders: Psychophysiological aspects. questions.question_text: In which scenario among the following circumstances would a diagnosis of substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder be appropriate for an patients who stopped taking benzodiazepines the previous day?

options.text: When anxiety is mild and limited to the withdrawal period.
Only when anxiety appears after the substance is fully eliminated from the body.
Anxiety is present that is sufficiently severe to warrant independent clinical attention.
Anxiety symptoms during withdrawal automatically qualify for an anxiety disorder.
The anxiety symptoms take complete precedence over any substance withdrawal diagnosis.

correct_answer.text: Anxiety is present that is sufficiently severe to warrant independent clinical attention.

questions.explanation: Anxiety symptoms commonly occur in substance intoxication and substance withdrawal. The diagnosis of the substance-specific intoxication or substance-specific withdrawal will usually suffice to categorize the symptom presentation. A diagnosis of substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder should be made in addition to substance intoxication or substance withdrawal only when the panic or anxiety symptoms are predominant in the clinical picture and are sufficiently severe to warrant independent clinical attention.

options.text: Decreased time spent in social situations

questions.explanation: In DSM5, a new chapter on disruptive, impulse control, and conduct disorders includes oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), conduct disorder (CD), intermittent explosive disorder (IED), pyromania, and kleptomania. This is a change from DSM-I V-T R, in which IED, pyromania, and kleptomania were included under “impulse control disorders not elsewhere classified,” and ODD and CD under “disorders first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence.” Trichotillomania (or skinpicking disorder) was previously included under “impulse control disorders not elsewhere classified” but has been recategorized to the obsessive– compulsive and related disorders label in DSM5.

questions.question_text: A woman who was abused keeps experiencing intrusive thoughts about past trauma when she returns home. According to ICD-11, which diagnosis is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Based on the information provided (intrusive thoughts about past trauma without mention of prolonged or repeated abuse, difficulty escaping situations, or disturbances in affect regulation, identity, or relationships), standard PTSD is most appropriate. Complex PTSD requires prolonged/repetitive trauma and additional symptoms of affect dysregulation, negative self-perception, and relationship difficulties.

questions.question_text: What is the primary difference in the clinical expression of generalized anxiety disorder across age groups?

options.text: A diagnosis of content of worry.
A diagnosis of degree of worry.
A diagnosis of patterns of comorbidity.
The degree of associated somatic versus cognitive symptoms.
A diagnosis of severity of impairment.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of content of worry.

questions.explanation: The clinical expression of generalized anxiety disorder is relatively consistent across the life span and the primary difference across age groups is the content of an individual’s worry. Children and adolescents tend to worry about school or sports performance, whereas adults are more likely to be concerned about their personal health or the well-being of their family.

questions.question_text: A 31-year-old patient presents 2 weeks after a car accident. They report anxiety symptoms and are unable to get into cars. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: At 2 weeks post-trauma, symptoms may resolve spontaneously. Active monitoring/watchful waiting is appropriate before diagnosing PTSD (requires 1 month of symptoms).

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old boy presents with acute onset of obsessive-compulsive symptoms and motor tics two weeks following a sore throat. His mother reports he had a positive throat culture for Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus. Which diagnostic criterion is NOT met for PANDAS?

options.text: Presence of OCD or tic disorder
Onset between 3 years and beginning of puberty

questions.explanation: Based on the case details: (1) he has both OCD symptoms and tics, (2) he is 9 years old (within the 3 years to puberty window), (3) he had acute onset, and (4) he had documented streptococcal infection temporally related to symptom onset. All five NICE diagnostic criteria for PANDAS would be met in this case.

questions.question_text: Which anxiety disorder shows a notable exception to the pattern of being more common in women than men?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states: all anxiety disorders are common in women than men. Notable exceptions are OCD, which is more in boys than girls, but equally common in adult men and women. This makes OCD unique in its sex distribution pattern.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the core distinguishing symptom cluster of major depressive disorder compared to anxiety disorders?

options.text: Depressed mood or loss of interest

correct_answer.text: Depressed mood or loss of interest

questions.explanation: While anxiety disorders are defined by core symptoms of excessive fear and worry, major depressive disorder is defined by depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure. Fatigue, psychomotor changes, sleep disturbance, and concentration difficulties are shared symptoms present in both conditions. It is precisely because these shared symptoms are so prominent that the two conditions are easily confused and frequently co-occur in clinical practice.

questions.question_text: A 63-year-old woman has been saving financial documents and records for many years, placing papers in piles throughout her apartment to the point where it has become unsafe. She acknowledges that the piles are a concern; however, she says that the papers encompasses important documents and she is afraid to throw them away. She recalls several instances in which her taxes were audited and she needed certain documents to avoid a penalty. She is concerned because her landlord is threatening to evict her unless she removes the piles of papers. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of nonpathological collecting behavior.
A diagnosis of dementia (major neurocognitive disorder).

questions.explanation: Although hoarding shares some features with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), research suggests that it is an independent disorder. DSM-5 recognizes hoarding disorder as a diagnosis; however, distinguishing individuals with hoarding disorder from those with OCD (who may hoard as a result of their disorder) can be difficult. This woman is worried about the harm that may ensue should she discard potentially important information. The focus on performing a ritual to prevent harm is more typical of OCD, whereas persons with hoarding disorder simply have difficulty discarding items that they have accumulated (i.e., the focus is on the hoarding itself). This woman appears to have insight into her behavior; thus, it is not delusional. However, it is clearly pathological because it is causing distress and potential Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 275 harm (i.e., eviction from her apartment). Patients with major neurocognitive disorder may develop symptoms characteristic of OCD as a result of the dementia, and this presentation would receive a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive and related disorder due to another medical condition. However, the patient in this vignette shows no evidence of cognitive decline.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old military veteran experiences severe flashbacks, avoidance of loud noises, and heightened startle responses. Additionally, he exhibits profound affective instability, holds a persistent negative belief about his own self-worth, and is entirely unable to sustain close relationships. According to ICD-11, which diagnosis best captures this complete clinical picture?
questions.explanation: Complex PTSD includes all core features of PTSD (re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal) but is differentiated by the additional presence of severe affect dysregulation, persistent negative self-concept, and relational difficulties, usually following repetitive, severe trauma.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes the course of hoarding disorder?

options.text: Hoarding behavior tends to wax and wane in severity throughout an patients’s life.
Hoarding behavior tends to improve steadily with aging.
Hoarding behavior tends to become more severe with increasing age.
Hoarding disorder typically remits completely by middle age.
Late-onset hoarding disorder has a better prognosis than early-onset.

correct_answer.text: Hoarding behavior tends to become more severe with increasing age.

questions.explanation: Hoarding tends to begin early in life and is generally chronic throughout a person’s life. The severity of the behavior increases with each decade of life.

questions.question_text: Why are psychopharmacological treatments for PTSD generally less effective than for other anxiety disorders?

options.text: PTSD patients are less compliant with pharmacological treatment than patients with other anxiety disorders
PTSD has a purely psychological aetiology that does not respond to pharmacological treatment
PTSD is so highly comorbid that treatments are more effectively aimed at comorbidities than at core PTSD symptoms, and PTSD-specific treatments have limited efficacy
The amygdala is not involved in PTSD, making standard anxiolytics ineffective
SSRIs are contraindicated in PTSD due to risk of traumatic memory reactivation

correct_answer.text: PTSD is so highly comorbid that treatments are more effectively aimed at comorbidities than at core PTSD symptoms, and PTSD-specific treatments have limited efficacy

questions.explanation: PTSD presents a particularly challenging treatment situation because of its high comorbidity with depression, insomnia, substance abuse, and pain disorders. Many pharmacological treatments are more effectively targeting these comorbidities rather than the core PTSD symptoms of re-experiencing, hyperarousal, and avoidance. Furthermore, PTSD-specific psychopharmacological treatments — even approved SSRIs — often leave patients with significant residual symptoms, meaning most PTSD patients require multimodal rather than monotherapy approaches.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes Complex PTSD from PTSD in ICD-11?

options.text: Low self-esteem and negative self-concept, along with affective dysregulation and interpersonal difficulties

correct_answer.text: Low self-esteem and negative self-concept, along with affective dysregulation and interpersonal difficulties

questions.explanation: Complex PTSD in ICD-11 includes all PTSD symptoms plus additional features: affective dysregulation, negative self-beliefs/low self-esteem, and interpersonal difficulties stemming from prolonged, repeated trauma.

questions.question_text: The characteristic symptom profile of panic disorder includes which combination?

options.text: Anticipatory anxiety, worry about panic attacks, unexpected panic attacks, and phobic avoidance
Generalised anxiety, fatigue, muscle tension, and irritability
Obsessions, compulsions, intrusive thoughts, and rituals
Re-experiencing, hyperarousal, sleep disturbance, and avoidance
Social performance anxiety, worry about exposure, expected panic attacks, and phobic avoidance

correct_answer.text: Anticipatory anxiety, worry about panic attacks, unexpected panic attacks, and phobic avoidance

questions.explanation: Panic disorder is characterised by core symptoms of anticipatory anxiety and worry specifically about having further panic attacks, with associated symptoms of unexpected panic attacks and phobic avoidance or behavioural change linked to concern about future attacks. The unexpected nature of panic attacks is a critical distinguishing feature — in social anxiety disorder, panic attacks are expected in specific social situations, making the predictability of attacks a key differential point.

questions.question_text: Following discharge from the hospital, a 22-year-old man describes vivid and intrusive memories of his stay in the intensive care unit (ICU), where he received treatment for smoke inhalation. Now at home, he states that he has memories of people being tortured and hearing their screams. He dreams of this every night, waking from sleep in a terror. He talks about not feeling like himself after the experience, finding little pleasure in life after what happened to him, and being easily angered by his family; in addition, he avoids his phyTrauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 63 sician out of fear that he will be told he needs to return to the ICU. What is the most likely explanation for this patient’s symptoms?

options.text: The man is experiencing depersonalization with flashbacks as a secondary symptom.
These symptoms indicate a primary dissociative disorder rather than PTSD.
Vivid and intrusive memories without nightmares do not meet PTSD criteria.
He had a delirium in the ICU and now has an adjustment disorder.
The symptoms are better explained by a primary anxiety disorder.

correct_answer.text: He had a delirium in the ICU and now has an adjustment disorder.

questions.explanation: Flashbacks in acute stress disorder must be distinguished from illusions, hallucinations, and other perceptual disturbances that may occur in schizophrenia, other psychotic disorders, depressive or bipolar disorder with psychotic features, a delirium, substance/medication-induced disorders, and psychotic disorders due to another medical condition. Acute stress disorder flashbacks are distinguished from these other perceptual disturbances by being directly related to the traumatic experience and occurring in the absence of other psychotic or substance/medication-induced features.

She acknowledges the piles are a concern but states the papers include important documents and she is afraid to throw them away to prevent harm. She recalls past tax audits where she needed documents to avoid a penalty. She is performing this saving ritual specifically to prevent a feared consequence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The focus on performing a ritual to prevent harm is more typical of OCD, whereas persons with hoarding disorder simply have difficulty discarding items that they have accumulated (i.e., the focus is on the hoarding itself).

Coworkers, doctors, and dentists regularly reassure him that his breath is fine, but he is convinced they are just being polite. He finds his worries intolerable. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder

correct_answer.text: Other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder

questions.explanation: Olfactory reference syndrome is characterized by excessive odor-related preoccupations and repetitive behaviors designed to address the odor sufficient to cause distress. Currently this disorder is classified under other specified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is shared between major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders?
questions.explanation: Major depressive disorder and anxiety disorders share several overlapping symptoms — specifically sleep disturbance, problems concentrating, fatigue, and psychomotor or arousal symptoms. These overlapping features explain why the two conditions are so frequently comorbid and why they can be difficult to distinguish clinically. The core symptoms of depression — depressed mood, loss of interest, guilt, worthlessness, suicidality, and appetite changes — are not shared with anxiety disorders and serve as the key distinguishing features.

questions.question_text: When called on at school, a 7-year-old boy will only nod or write in response. The family of the child is surprised to hear this from the teacher, because the boy speaks normally when at home with his parents. The child has achieved appropriate developmental milestones, and a medical evaluation indicates that he is healthy. The boy is unable to give any explanation for his behavior, but the parents are concerned that it will affect his school performance. What diagnosis most accurately describes this child’s symptoms?

options.text: A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder.

questions.explanation: When encountering other individuals in social interactions, children with selective mutism do not initiate speech or reciprocally respond when spoken to. Lack of speech occurs in social interactions with children or adults. Children with selective mutism will speak in their home in the presence of immediate family members but often not even in front of close friends or seconddegree relatives, such as grandparents or cousins. The disturbance is often marked by high social anxiety. Children with selective mutism often refuse to speak at school, leading to academic or educational impairment, as teachers often find it difficult to assess skills such as reading. The lack of speech may interfere with social communication, although children with this disorder sometimes use nonspoken or nonverbal means (e.g., grunting, pointing, writing) to communicate and may be willing or eager to perform or engage in social encounters when speech is not required (e.g., nonverbal parts in school plays).

questions.question_text: Complex PTSD is differentiated from PTSD primarily by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Complex PTSD is characterized by persistent difficulties in sustaining relationships and in feeling close to others, in addition to severe and pervasive problems in affect regulation and persistent negative self-beliefs. Poor interpersonal relationships are a key distinguishing feature from standard PTSD.

questions.question_text: The fact that all anxiety disorders share core symptoms of fear and worry, and are largely treated with the same drugs, raises which important conceptual question?

options.text: It implies that anxiety disorders are entirely fictional diagnostic categories
It proves that diagnosis is irrelevant and treatment should never be individualised
It raises the question of whether different anxiety disorders are truly distinct entities or different aspects of the same underlying illness
It supports the exclusive use of benzodiazepines for all anxiety subtypes
It validates the DSM categorical approach over dimensional models

correct_answer.text: It raises the question of whether different anxiety disorders are truly distinct entities or different aspects of the same underlying illness

questions.explanation: When multiple diagnostic categories share the same core symptoms, respond to the same drugs, and involve the same neurobiological circuits, it challenges the validity of treating them as entirely separate diseases. This has driven an ongoing debate in psychiatry about whether the anxiety disorders — and indeed anxiety and depression together — are better understood as overlapping dimensions of a shared psychopathological spectrum rather than as discrete categorical entities.

questions.question_text: Prolonged Exposure treatment involves the use of:
questions.explanation: Prolonged Exposure Therapy involves the use of both imaginal exposure and in vivo exposure. That is, patients listen to audiotaped sessions involving their verbal narrative of trauma accounts repeatedly during the therapy, as well as doing activities that they usually avoid due to their PTSD. A sleep diary is not part of the Prolonged Exposure Therapy protocol, which generally lasts for about 10 sessions.

She reports a rapid heartbeat, lasting a few minutes at a time, multiple days a week for the past few months. She presents to the emergency room after another episode. Which medical test should be obtained to rule out an organic cause for this disorder?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain

questions.explanation: Mitral valve prolapse can be associated with panic disorder, as it can cause heart palpitations, dyspnea, fear, and anxiety. An EKG should be obtained to rule out mitral valve prolapse in cases of panic disorder.

questions.question_text: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department suffering from a sudden, severe surge of panic. He has no prior diagnosis of panic disorder, but he reports taking several doses of an over-the-counter cold medication earlier that day. which of the following options clinical features, if present in this case, would help to confirm a diagnosis of substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder?

options.text: Symptoms that cause only minimal distress to the individual.
Symptoms that appear weeks or months after substance/medication use ends.
Symptoms that are less intense than would normally result from the substance/medication.
Symptoms that include significant cognitive impairment or disorientation.
Lack of any prior diagnosis of anxiety disorder or panic symptoms.

correct_answer.text: Lack of any prior diagnosis of anxiety disorder or panic symptoms.

questions.explanation: Many substances can potentially cause anxiety symptoms, and it can sometimes be difficult to determine whether medication use is etiologically related to the onset of anxiety symptoms. Evidence to support the presence of a substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder includes temporal associations and symptoms that are consistent with the medication and dose. By definition, a substance/medication-induced anxiety disorder must cause significant distress or impairment in functioning, and it cannot occur exclusively during the course of a delirium.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man is referred to a psychiatrist by his primary care doctor after mentioning to the doctor that he routinely spends a lot of time pulling out facial hair with tweezers, even after carefully shaving. On evaluation, he admits to frequent pulling of his facial hair, consuming significant amount of time; he explains that he becomes anxious when looking at himself because his moustache, hairline, and sideburns are asymmetrical. He pulls out hairs in an effort to make them more symmetrical, but is rarely satisfied with the results. He finds this very upsetting but cannot resist the urge to try and “fix” his facial hair. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD).
A diagnosis of delusional disorder, somatic type.
A diagnosis of normal age-appropriate appearance concerns.

questions.explanation: In the case of repetitive hair pulling, distinguishing among trichotillomania, BDD, and OCD can sometimes be difficult. The differential diagnosis rests on the reasons for the pulling. Trichotillomania generally stems Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 281 from boredom or anxiety, whereas BDD-related hair pulling is generally associated with perceived ugliness of the hair. When the pulling is in the service of symmetry, OCD is the more appropriate diagnosis. Further examination of the individual would likely reveal additional examples of his preoccupation with symmetry. Although some amount of hair pulling may be normal, the degree and the distress caused make normal age-appropriate appearance concerns an unlikely explanation in this case. Psychotic disorders should be ruled out—in this vignette, the patient’s symptoms appear to be more a preoccupation than a delusion.

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old woman is referred to a psychiatrist by her internist after she admits to him that she recurrently pulls hair from her eyebrows to the point that she has scarring and there is little or no eyebrow hair left. She states that her natural eyebrows are “bushy” and “repulsive” and that she “looks like a caveman.” A photograph of the woman before she began pulling her eyebrow hair shows a normal-looking teenager. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder.
A diagnosis of delusional disorder, somatic type.
A diagnosis of normal age-appropriate appearance concerns.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder.

questions.explanation: There can be a variety of causes for hair pulling. Individuals with trichotillomania pull hair out of anxiety or boredom; the behavior provides distraction, pleasure, or a relief from anxiety. When hair pulling is purely for the purpose of improving a perceived defect in appearance, the behavior is better conceptualized as symptomatic of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). As with other presentations of BDD, insight into the behavior can be poor, and the belief can reach delusional levels. If the delusions are limited to the appearance concerns, an additional diagnosis is not necessary. The behavior is similar to obsessive-compulsive disorder; however, the focus on appearance is diagnostic for BDD. It may be normal for teenagers to be concerned about their appearance; however, the fact that this patient has pulled her hair to the point of causing scarring makes this a pathological behavior.

questions.question_text: Which feature best differentiates body dysmorphic disorder from obsessive-compulsive disorder?

options.text: In OCD, beliefs about obsessions are ego-dystonic
In BDD, preoccupation is limited to appearance

correct_answer.text: In BDD, preoccupation is limited to appearance

questions.explanation: In body dysmorphic disorder, the preoccupation and repetitive behaviors focus specifically on perceived appearance defects, whereas in OCD the obsessions and compulsions can involve any content.

questions.explanation: Individuals with excoriation disorder have recurrent skin-picking behaviors that are severe enough to cause skin lesions. It is not necessary that the behavior cause deformity.

For instance, fentanyl, buprenorphine, and methadone require assays for these substances in particular given structural differences relative to naturally occurring opioids (i.e., opiates), including morphine and codeine. Of note, all agents that activate mu receptors are known as opioids (literally, “resembling opiates”), and agonists that are structurally related to compounds derived from opium poppy are opiates proper. The DSM5 uses the more encompassing term opioid, as in “opioid use disorder” and “opioid withdrawal.”

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes the course of excoriation (skin-picking) disorder?

options.text: Skin-picking behavior tends to wax and wane in severity throughout an patients’s life.
Skin-picking behavior improves significantly in young adulthood.
Excoriation disorder is typically more severe in middle-aged individuals.
Skin-picking behavior resolves spontaneously by adulthood in most cases.
Excoriation disorder is milder and more treatable when onset occurs in later life.

correct_answer.text: Skin-picking behavior tends to wax and wane in severity throughout an patients’s life.

questions.explanation: Although it can begin at any age, excoriation disorder usually begins during adolescence, coincident with the onset of puberty, and is frequently triggered by skin conditions such as acne. The disorder usually has a chronic course with some waxing and waning if untreated. In some cases, the disorder may come and go for weeks, months, or even years at a time.

questions.question_text: A 9-year-old boy cannot go to sleep without having a parent in his room. While falling asleep, he frequently awakens to check that a parent is still there. One parent commonly stays until the boy falls asleep. If he wakes up alone during the night, he starts to panic and gets up to find his parents. He also reports frequent nightmares in which he or his parents are harmed. He occasionally calls out that he saw a strange figure peering into his dark room. The parents commonly wake in the morning to find the boy asleep on the floor of their room. They once tried to leave him with a relative so they could go on a vacation; however, he became so distressed in anticipation of this that they canceled their plans. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of separation anxiety disorder is excessive anxiety about being separated from home or attachment figures, beyond what would be expected for the person’s developmental stage. By definition, it firsts presents before age 18; however, it may continue into adulthood. Typical presentations include reluctance to leave home or even stay in a room without a parent. In the latter case, children frequently have difficulty at bedtime and may insist that a parent stay with them. questions.question_text: According to the natural history of anxiety disorders, which pattern best describes how these conditions evolve over time?

Linear progression from subsyndromal to full syndrome without remission

Rather than following a linear or stable course, they tend to fluctuate — evolving into full syndrome expression, receding to subsyndromal levels, and re-emerging as the same disorder, a different anxiety disorder subtype, or as major depression. questions.question_text: Among the following options, which statements best describes how panic attacks differ from panic disorder?

Panic attacks can only be linked to medical conditions such as asthma or seizure disorders.

correct_answer.text: Panic attacks represent a syndrome that can occur with a variety of other disorders.

questions.explanation: Panic attacks are abrupt surges of intense fear or intense discomfort that reach a peak within minutes, accompanied by physical and/or cognitive symptoms. Panic attacks may be either expected (e.g., in response to a typically feared object or situation) or unexpected (meaning that the panic attack occurs for no apparent reason). Although DSM-5 defines symptoms for the purpose of identifying a panic attack, panic attack is not a mental disorder and cannot be coded. Panic attacks can occur in the context of any anxiety disorder as well as other mental disorders (e.g., depressive disorders, posttraumatic stress disorder, substance use disorders) and some medical conditions (e.g., cardiac, respiratory, vestibular, gastrointestinal). When the presence of a panic attack is identified, it should be noted as a specifier (e.g., “posttraumatic stress disorder with panic attacks”). For panic disorder, the presence of panic attack is contained within the criteria for the disorder, and panic attack is not used as a specifier.

questions.question_text: The disruption of sleep is a core feature in what anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation: Though someone experiencing a panic attack during the night would most likely experience a disruption in sleep, as would someone who encountered the trigger of a specific phobia at night, only for generalized anxiety disorder is sleep disruption a criterion in and of itself.

questions.question_text: Anxiety triggered internally from traumatic memories stored in the hippocampus activating the amygdala is termed re-experiencing and is particularly associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: Re-experiencing is a process by which traumatic memories stored in the hippocampus activate the amygdala without any external trigger, generating a full fear response. This internal triggering mechanism is central to PTSD, where patients relive traumatic experiences — through flashbacks, nightmares, or intrusive memories — triggered by sensory cues associated with the original trauma. This contrasts with the externally-triggered fears of phobias and social anxiety.

questions.question_text: A individual was stabbed by his coworker at work 15 days ago. After the assault he developed intense anxiety about going back to work. He says he has not been able to sleep well since the attack due to nightmares of the event. He ruminates daily about the assault, often experiencing it as if it were happening again. He is constantly “on edge” about the possibility of strangers attacking him. Which of the following diagnoses is most consistent with his presentation?

options.text: A diagnosis of acute stress disorder
A diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of acute stress disorder

ASD develops within 3 days to 1 month of the occurrence of the trauma and resolves within a month of the index trauma. If the symptoms persist for more than 1 month, the diagnosis of PTSD is made. Although ASD may remit within a month, it can also progress to PTSD. Half of patients suffering from PTSD report symptoms of ASD preceding PTSD. questions.question_text: Although gambling can seem compulsive, gambling disorder is not considered a type of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) for which of the following reasons?

options.text: A person with gambling disorder derives direct pleasure from the behavior.
Patients with gambling disorder have poorer insight into their irrational behavior.
Gambling disorder is best categorized as a behavioral addiction rather than a compulsive behavior.
The repetitive behavior linked to gambling is meant to avoid anxiety.
In gambling disorder, patients have control over their repetitive behaviors.

correct_answer.text: A person with gambling disorder derives direct pleasure from the behavior.

questions.explanation: Although a number of behaviors, such as gambling or sexual behavior, can seem compulsive, gambling disorder and sexual paraphilias differ from OCD in that the compulsive behaviors associated with OCD are meant to decrease anxiety, whereas in the other disorders they are a source of direct pleasure. Individuals with gambling disorder seek treatment mainly out of concern for the deleterious consequences of their behavior. In both gambling disorder and OCD, the level of insight into the behavior can vary, but like individuals with OCD, those with gambling disorder cannot control their gambling.

questions.question_text: Although onset of a specific phobia can occur at any age, specific phobia most generally develops during which age period?
questions.explanation: Specific phobia usually develops in early childhood, with the majority of cases developing prior to age 10 years. The median age at onset is between 7 and 11 years, with the mean at about 10 years. Situational specific phobias tend to have a later age at onset than do natural environment, animal, or blood-injection-injury specific phobias. Specific phobias that develop in childhood and adolescence are likely to wax and wane during that period. However, phobias that persist into adulthood are unlikely to remit for the majority of individuals. When specific phobia is being diagnosed in children, two issues should be considered. First, young children may express their fear and anxiety by crying, tantrums, freezing, or clinging. Second, young children typically are not able to understand the concept of avoidance. Therefore, the clinician should assemble additional information from parents, teachers, or others who know the child well.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with intrusive thoughts about contamination, leading her to wash her hands excessively throughout the day, causing significant functional impairment. She has not received prior psychiatric treatment. According to NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate initial management step?

options.text: Prescribe an SSRI immediately at maximum therapeutic dose
Prescribe a benzodiazepine for acute anxiety relief
Assess severity and consider psychological therapy (CBT with ERP) as first-line treatment

correct_answer.text: Assess severity and consider psychological therapy (CBT with ERP) as first-line treatment

questions.explanation: That Psychological therapy is more effective than pharmacological therapy and should be used as first line where possible and recommends a comprehensive assessment considering distress and functional impairment. For a patient with significant functional impairment and no prior treatment, CBT with ERP represents the evidence-based first-line intervention before pharmacotherapy.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient psychiatrist by his parents because of a fear of dogs and thunderstorms. When he encounters one of them he starts breathing heavily, sweating, complaining of chest pain, and feeling dizzy. As they live in an area frequented by storms, he has “a panic attack” three or four times a week. The first time the symptoms occurred 3 months ago, his parents took him to the emergency department out of fear that he was having a heart attack. The workup was negative, and he was given an antianxiety agent to take on as as-needed basis, which they have been refilling through his primary care physician. Since then, he has always carried the medication with him and insists on returning home if he realizes he does not have it. The school nurse has a supply of the medication in case he needs it. He avoids sleepovers out of fear of being embarrassed in front of his peers if he encounters one of the stressors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Though the child shows the same symptoms as those of a panic attack, and may indeed be having full-blown panic attacks, he cannot be diagnosed with panic disorder, as the attacks are not unexpected. Because there are circumscribed triggers, specific phobia is the most likely diagnosis.

questions.question_text: At what mean age of onset does generalized anxiety disorder typically first present?
questions.explanation: The source clearly states GAD – 30 years when listing the mean age of onset for various anxiety disorders, making this a straightforward factual recall question.

questions.question_text: How long after a loss event can Prolonged Grief Disorder be diagnosed?
questions.explanation: Prolonged Grief Disorder can be diagnosed when grief response has persisted for more than 6 months at a minimum and clearly exceeds expected social, cultural or religious norms.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best illustrates the principle that all anxiety disorders share the same circuits but differ in the pattern of circuit dysfunction?

options.text: GAD is treated with SSRIs while panic disorder is treated with benzodiazepines — reflecting different neurotransmitters
GAD involves persistent low-level amygdala and CSTC dysfunction, while panic disorder involves intermittent catastrophic unexpected dysfunction, within the same shared circuits
PTSD is caused by hippocampal damage while GAD reflects genetic variation in GABA-A receptors
Social anxiety disorder affects the DLPFC while GAD affects the amygdala — different circuits
The different anxiety disorders respond to different drug classes, confirming they involve distinct circuits

correct_answer.text: GAD involves persistent low-level amygdala and CSTC dysfunction, while panic disorder involves intermittent catastrophic unexpected dysfunction, within the same shared circuits

questions.explanation: The chapter's key neurobiological argument is that different anxiety disorders are not produced by different circuits or different neurotransmitters, but by different patterns of malfunctioning within the same circuits. GAD represents persistent, unremitting but not severe dysfunction. Panic disorder represents intermittent, catastrophic, unexpected dysfunction. Social anxiety involves expected catastrophic dysfunction. PTSD reflects traumatically conditioned dysfunction. All of these patterns occur within the same shared amygdala-CSTC framework.

questions.question_text: After a routine chest X ray, a 53-year-old man with a prior diagnosis of heavy cigarette use is told that he has a suspicious lesion in his lung. A bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis of adenocarcinoma. The man delays scheduling a follow-up appointment with the oncologist for more than 2 weeks, describes feeling as if “all of this is not real,” is having nightly dreams of seeing his own tombstone, and is experiencing intrusive flashbacks to the moment when he heard the physician saying, “The tests strongly suggest that you have cancer of the lung.” He is tearful and is convinced he will die. He also feels intense guilt that his smoking caused the cancer and expresses the thought that he “deserves” to have cancer. What diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical picture?

options.text: A diagnosis of acute stress disorder.
A diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder.
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of acute stress disorder (ASD) is the development of characteristic symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month following exposure to one or more traumatic events. Traumatic events that are experienced directly include, but are not limited to, exposure to war as a combatant Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 289 or civilian, threatened or actual violent personal assault (e.g., sexual assault, physical attack, active combat, mugging, childhood physical and/or sexual abuse, being kidnapped, being taken hostage, terrorist attack, or torture), natural or human-made disasters (e.g., earthquake, hurricane, airplane crash), and severe accidents (e.g., severe motor vehicle or industrial accident). A lifethreatening illness or debilitating condition is not necessarily considered a traumatic event. Stressful events that do not meet Criterion A definitions for a diagnosis of ASD may nonetheless be sufficient to qualify for an adjustment disorder diagnosis.

questions.question_text: He denies ever experiencing such symptoms in the past. His medical history is significant for treated hypothyroidism and family history of panic disorder in his mother. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of substanceinduced anxiety disorder
Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition
A diagnosis of unspecified anxiety disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of substanceinduced anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: The patient has suffered a panic attack induced by cocaine as evidenced by the temporal correlation of symptoms with use. Substanceor medicationinduced anxiety disorder is diagnosed when a panic attack or anxiety is the predominant symptom and develops during or soon after substance or medication intoxication or withdrawal. The substance or medication has to be capable of producing the symptom, and the symptom should not be better explained by an anxiety disorder that is not substance induced. Many medical conditions cause anxiety and panic attacks. Examples include endocrine diseases (e.g., hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, hyperadrenocortisolism, hypoglycemia), cardiovascular disorders (e.g., congestive heart failure, pulmonary embolism, arrhythmia), respiratory illness (e.g., chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, pneumonia), metabolic disturbances (e.g., vitamin B12 deficiency, porphyria), and neurological illness (e.g., neoplasms, vestibular dysfunction, encephalitis, seizure disorders). The other options are less likely given the temporal correlation of the attack with substance use as well as the lack of prior episodes. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). options.text: Fear of strangers and separation from caregivers

correct_answer.text: Fear of strangers and separation from caregivers

questions.explanation: Separation anxiety disorder is characterized by fear of separation from caregivers and develops toward the end of the first year. Normal developmental fears follow an ontogenetic pattern where different fears are prominent at different ages. Fear of strangers and emergence of separation anxiety are prominent toward the end of the first year.
