questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms are considered manifestations of the worry dimension of anxiety, linked to CSTC circuit dysfunction?

options.text: Increased heart rate, blood pressure, and diaphoresis
Anxious misery, apprehensive expectations, catastrophic thinking, and obsessions
Phobic avoidance, anticipatory anxiety, and panic attacks
Shortness of breath, smothering sensations, and hyperventilation

correct_answer.text: Anxious misery, apprehensive expectations, catastrophic thinking, and obsessions

questions.explanation: The worry dimension of anxiety encompasses sustained, ruminative cognitive symptoms — anxious misery, apprehensive expectation, catastrophic thinking, and obsessions. These reflect overactivation of CSTC feedback loops from the prefrontal cortex. Similar loops are also hypothesised to regulate ruminations and delusions, suggesting that these symptoms exist on a spectrum of recurrent, intrusive thought pathology sharing a common circuit substrate.

questions.question_text: In what aspect of generalized anxiety disorder do men and women most commonly differ?

options.text: A diagnosis of degree of impairment.
A diagnosis of patterns of comorbidity.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of patterns of comorbidity.

questions.explanation: Women and men with generalized anxiety disorder tend to have similar symptoms and presentation; however, they have different patterns of comorbidity consistent with gender differences in the prevalence of mental disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct regarding separation anxiety disorder?
questions.explanation: Separation anxiety disorder requires a duration of at least 6 months for diagnosis; while it typically begins in childhood, the minimum duration criterion is a key diagnostic feature.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

A diagnosis of social anxiety disorder
A diagnosis of schizoid personality disorder

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man reports episodes in which he suddenly and unexpectedly awakens from sleep feeling a surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes. During this time, he feels short of breath and has heart palpitations, sweating, and nausea. His medical history is significant only for well-controlled hypertension. He has begun to have anticipatory anxiety associated with going to sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition

questions.explanation: Nocturnal panic attacks associated with sleep are an example of an unexpected panic attack. The presence of sudden, unexpected panic attacks in the absence of a medical disorder driving the attacks is the main feature of panic disorder. His well-controlled hypertension is unlikely to be the cause.

questions.question_text: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by which of the following features?

options.text: Symptoms must appear immediately upon exposure to stressor
Maladaptive reaction to identifiable psychosocial stressor(s) emerging within one month
Symptoms must persist for at least 6 months
Symptoms indicate another specific mental disorder

correct_answer.text: Maladaptive reaction to identifiable psychosocial stressor(s) emerging within one month

questions.explanation: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by a maladaptive reaction to an identifiable psychosocial stressor or multiple stressors that usually emerges within a month, with symptoms including preoccupation with the stressor and failure to adapt, causing significant functional impairment.

questions.question_text: Panic attacks, on average, last what length of time?
questions.explanation: . 20 to 30 minutes. Panic attacks typically begin with physiologic symptoms of sweating, tachycardia, shaking, and shortness of breath, as well as psychological symptoms of impending doom and a feeling that something is wrong. These symptoms usually peak in about 10 minutes before resolving over the period of the next 10 to 20 minutes, for an average total length of 20 to 30 minutes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following additional comorbidities are anxiety disorders frequently associated with, beyond major depression?

options.text: Autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability
Bipolar disorder, ADHD, substance abuse, pain disorders, and sleep disorders
Eating disorders and personality disorders exclusively
Psychosis and delirium in elderly patients
Tourette syndrome and tic disorders predominantly

correct_answer.text: Bipolar disorder, ADHD, substance abuse, pain disorders, and sleep disorders

questions.explanation: Anxiety disorders carry a broad comorbidity burden. Beyond their frequent co-occurrence with major depression, they are commonly comorbid with substance abuse, ADHD, bipolar disorder, pain disorders, and sleep disorders. This wide comorbidity profile has important clinical implications — it means that a symptom-based treatment approach, targeting specific malfunctioning brain circuits, is often more practical than trying to treat each diagnostic category in isolation.

questions.question_text: Which overarching principle best summarises the neurobiological basis for why the same pharmacological agents — SSRIs, SNRIs, benzodiazepines, and alpha-2-delta ligands — are effective across multiple different anxiety disorder subtypes?

options.text: All anxiety disorders share the same genetic polymorphisms in serotonin transporter genes
All anxiety disorders are caused by the same environmental stressors and respond to the same psychological interventions
All anxiety disorders involve the same core circuits — amygdala-centred fear circuits and CSTC worry loops — regulated by the same neurotransmitters, making shared pharmacological targets rational
Anxiety disorders are not truly different conditions, so any anxiolytic agent will work for all of them equally
The placebo effect accounts for most pharmacological efficacy across anxiety disorder subtypes

correct_answer.text: All anxiety disorders involve the same core circuits — amygdala-centred fear circuits and CSTC worry loops — regulated by the same neurotransmitters, making shared pharmacological targets rational

questions.explanation: The shared pharmacological treatment landscape across anxiety disorders is not coincidental — it directly reflects shared neurobiology. All anxiety disorder subtypes involve dysregulation of the same two core circuits: the amygdala-centred fear circuit and the CSTC worry loop. Both circuits are regulated by the same set of neurotransmitters — serotonin, GABA, glutamate, norepinephrine, and voltage-gated ion channels. Treatments that modulate these shared targets therefore produce anxiolytic benefit across all subtypes, regardless of the specific pattern of dysfunction within those circuits.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes risk and prognostic factors in hoarding disorder?

options.text: About 10% of patients who hoard report having a relative who also hoards.
Approximately half of the variability in hoarding behavior is due to genetic factors. Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 57
Separation insecurity is a prominent temperamental feature of patients with hoarding disorder and their first-degree relatives.
Hoarding disorder has been linked to high rates of childhood neglect and abuse.
Hoarding disorder has no genetic basis and is purely a learned behavior.

correct_answer.text: Approximately half of the variability in hoarding behavior is due to genetic factors. Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 57

questions.explanation: Hoarding behavior is familial, with about 50% of individuals who hoard reporting having a relative who also hoards. Twin studies indicate that approximately 50% of the variability in hoarding behavior is attributable to additive genetic factors. Indecisiveness is a prominent temperamental feature of individuals with hoarding disorder and their first-degree relatives. Individuals with hoarding disorder often retrospectively report stressful and traumatic life events preceding the onset of the disorder or causing an exacerbation.

questions.question_text: Which statement most accurately characterizes compulsive behaviors in obsessivecompulsive disorder (OCD)?

options.text: Compulsions are experienced as pleasurable by most individuals with OCD.
Compulsive behaviors in OCD are aimed at reducing the distress triggered by obsessions.
Examples of compulsive behaviors encompasses paraphilias (sexual compulsions), gambling, and substance use.
Obsessions are repetitive ritualistic behaviors performed to reduce anxiety.
Compulsive behaviors in OCD are generally goal directed, fulfilling a realistic purpose.

correct_answer.text: Compulsive behaviors in OCD are aimed at reducing the distress triggered by obsessions.

questions.explanation: Obsessions are repetitive and persistent thoughts (e.g., of contamination), images (e.g., of violent or horrific scenes), or urges (e.g., to stab someone). Compulsions (or rituals) are repetitive behaviors (e.g., washing, checking) or mental acts (e.g., counting, repeating words silently) that the individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly. Most individuals with OCD have both obsessions and compulsions. Compulsions are typically performed in response to an obsession (e.g., thoughts of contamination leading to washing rituals or that something is incorrect leading to repeating rituals until it feels “just right”). The aim is to reduce the distress triggered by obsessions or to prevent a feared event (e.g., becoming ill). However, these compulsions either are not connected in a realistic way to the feared event (e.g., arranging items symmetrically to prevent harm to a loved one) or are clearly excessive (e.g., showering for hours each day). Compulsions are not done for pleasure, although some individuals experience relief from anxiety or distress. Certain behaviors are sometimes described as “compulsive,” including sexual behavior (in the case of paraphilias), gambling (i.e., gambling disorder), and substance use (e.g., alcohol use disorder). However, these behaviors differ from the compulsions of OCD in that the person usually derives pleasure from Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 273 the activity and may wish to resist it only because of its deleterious consequences.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best represents the two core symptoms shared across all anxiety disorder subtypes?
questions.explanation: Anxiety as a clinical phenomenon can be deconstructed into two fundamental symptom dimensions. Fear encompasses discrete manifestations such as panic and phobia — responses to perceived threat. Worry encompasses more sustained cognitive symptoms including anxious misery, apprehensive expectation, and obsessions. These two dimensions are not only clinically distinct but are also regulated by separate neurobiological circuits: fear by the amygdala-centred circuit, and worry by the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop.

questions.question_text: What is a key difference between Complex PTSD and PTSD?

options.text: Complex PTSD involves only re-experiencing symptoms
Complex PTSD includes poor interpersonal relationships and decreased self-worth
Complex PTSD responds better to medication
Complex PTSD occurs only after single-incident trauma

correct_answer.text: Complex PTSD includes poor interpersonal relationships and decreased self-worth

questions.explanation: Complex PTSD differs from PTSD by including symptoms such as decreased self-worth, affective dysregulation, and poor interpersonal relationships, typically resulting from repetitive exposure to trauma.

questions.question_text: In addition to negative mood, two symptoms from which of the following criteria must be met for a diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?
questions.explanation: In addition to a history of exposure to trauma, a PTSD diagnosis requires one symptom of intrusion (i.e., reenactment, nightmares, dissociative responses, etc.), one of avoidance (i.e., avoiding memories or external reminders of the trauma), two symptoms of negative mood/cognition (i.e., negative perceptions of self, cognitive distortions, excessive guilt, decreased interest in activities, etc.), and two in arousal alterations.

questions.question_text: PTSD is now categorised in some diagnostic systems as which type of disorder?

options.text: Stress-related disorder and disorder of hyperarousal

correct_answer.text: Stress-related disorder and disorder of hyperarousal

questions.explanation: PTSD has been reclassified in some modern diagnostic systems away from the anxiety disorders category and is now considered a stress-related disorder. It is also specifically characterised as a disorder of hyperarousal. Its core symptoms — anxiety while re-experiencing the traumatic event, worry, increased arousal and exaggerated startle responses, sleep disturbance including nightmares, and avoidance behaviours — reflect this hyperarousal and trauma-conditioned nature.

questions.question_text: What is the lifetime prevalence of OCD?
questions.explanation: The source clearly states The lifetime prevalence of OCD is fairly constant – around 2-3%, establishing this as the standard lifetime prevalence figure for the disorder.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old woman reports sudden, unexpected episodes of intense anxiety, accompanied by headaches, a rapid pulse, nausea, and shortness of breath. During the episodes she fears that she is dying, and she has presented several times to emergency departments. Each time she has been told that she is medically healthy; she is commonly reassured for a time, but on the occurrence of a new episode she again becomes concerned that she has some severe medical problem. She was given lorazepam once but disliked the sedating effect and has not taken it again. She abstains from all medications and alcohol in an attempt to minimize potential causes for her attacks. What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?

options.text: A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.
Anxiety due to another medical condition.
A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: The presence of sudden, unexpected panic attacks in the absence of a medical disorder is the main feature of panic disorder. In addition to worries about the attacks, many individuals report broader concerns about health and mental health outcomes. In a search for an explanation for their symptoms, they may worry about having a major disease. This differs from illness anxiety disorder in that the concern with panic attacks stems from what might be seen as a reasonable concern over their dramatic and unexplained symptoms; patients with panic attacks do not show the preoccupation with having a feared disease that is typical of illness anxiety disorder (or hypochondriasis in DSMIV). Specific phobia refers to anxiety centered on a specific trigger.

questions.question_text: In excoriation (skin-picking) disorder, which of the following is the most typical motivation for the skin-picking behavior?

options.text: Self-punishment to manage guilt and shame.
A diagnosis of fear of infection.

questions.explanation: Individuals with excoriation disorder usually pick their skin out of anxiety or boredom. Skin picking to fix imaginary defects in appearance would suggest body dysmorphic disorder, and picking to fix defects in symmetry or to prevent infection would suggest obsessive-compulsive disorder. Skin picking in excoriation disorder is not comparable to self-mutilative behavior that occurs in the context of dissociative experiences or borderline personality disorder.

questions.question_text: A 48-year-old man explains that he likes to collect wine and claims many bottles are valuable. However, he rarely drinks the wine and has never sold or given any away because he finds it hard to part with the bottles. He has used increasing portions of his house for storage, causing severe financial hardship and distress to his wife. He admits many bottles have spoiled due to improper storage but still refuses to discard them. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: His difficulty parting with or drinking the wine, the fact that his acquisition exceeds his ability to store the wine, and his wife’s distress make hoarding disorder the most likely diagnosis. Because his acquisition involves buying objects not needed and for which there is no space, the excessive acquisition specifier is added.

questions.question_text: A lack of specificity in which criteria is a potential challenge in diagnosing someone with an adjustment disorder?
questions.explanation: One of the challenges in diagnosing an adjustment disorder is that there are no clear criteria that define the stressors that are required to make this diagnosis and specific affective, cognitive, and autonomic descriptions are not specified. Another challenge is that the symptoms can be of any severity.

questions.question_text: Generalised anxiety disorder, compared to panic disorder, is characterised by circuit malfunctioning that is best described as:

options.text: Intermittent and catastrophic in a predictable, expected manner
Intermittent and catastrophic in an unexpected manner
Traumatic in origin and conditioned through repeated exposure
Variable and episodic, linked to discrete phobic stimuli

questions.explanation: Different anxiety disorders represent distinct patterns of dysfunction within the same shared neurobiological circuits, rather than different circuits altogether. In GAD, the malfunctioning is hypothetically persistent and unremitting but not severe — a chronic low-level dysregulation. In contrast, panic disorder involves intermittent but catastrophically intense dysfunction occurring unexpectedly, social anxiety involves expected catastrophic dysfunction in social contexts, and PTSD reflects dysfunction that is traumatically conditioned.

questions.question_text: Which brain region is most implicated in PTSD pathophysiology?
questions.explanation: The amygdala is most implicated in PTSD, particularly due to its role in fear responses and consolidation of emotional memories. PTSD patients typically show reduced bilateral amygdala volume.

questions.question_text: The gender ratio of OCD in clinical samples is approximately:
questions.explanation: The gender ratio of OCD in clinical samples is roughly equal, indicating approximately 1:1 ratio, though females predominate in community populations at approximately 1.5:1.

questions.question_text: How many Criterion B symptoms are required to be present for the diagnosis of acute stress disorder?
questions.explanation: Criterion B for acute stress disorder requires the presence of 9 (or more) of a total of 12 symptoms from any of the five categories of intrusion, negative mood, dissociation, avoidance, and arousal, beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred.
